label: Edu-ConvoKit: talk time and math density
summary: The learner's share of the words in their conversation with the AI, and how many terms from Edu-ConvoKit's math glossary the learner and the AI use per message. Edu-ConvoKit computes them on this computer, with no model.
cite: Wang, R. E., & Demszky, D. (2024). Edu-ConvoKit: An Open-Source Library for Education Conversation Data. NAACL 2024 (System Demonstrations), 61-69. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2024.naacl-demo.6
attribution: Edu-ConvoKit (Wang & Demszky, 2024). Its math density follows Himmelsbach, Hill, Liu & Demszky (2024), A Quantitative Study of Mathematical Language in Upper Elementary Classrooms, EdWorkingPaper 24-1029.

evidence.original: Talk time counts words. Math density counts terms from a glossary of math vocabulary; measured that way in 1,657 4th and 5th grade lessons, teachers who used more mathematical language were more effective at raising students' test scores (Himmelsbach et al., 2024).
evidence.integration: Its fixtures pass through the adapter with Edu-ConvoKit 0.4.0, and through the harness's measure call. Not compared with anything on learners' chats with an AI.
evidence.unknown: What these numbers say about a learner's chat with an AI, where the AI writes most of the words; nobody has related them to learning there.

risk_notes: A number can mislead a teacher: the glossary holds everyday words such as line, value and total, and a short chat gives a number that means little. It runs on this computer, calls no model and sends nothing elsewhere.
